faq.q: What is the difference between markup and margin?

faq.q: How often should you reprice?

faq.q: How do you calculate markup on a product?
faq.a: Take the price, subtract the cost, then divide by the cost. A $22.00 case sold at $33.00 keeps $11.00, so the markup is 50%. Divide the same $11.00 by the $33.00 price and you get a 33.3% margin, which is what your P&L reports.

faq.q: Is it better to use markup or margin?
faq.a: Set the target in margin, then price in markup. Margin is the share of the price you keep, so 30% of a $31.43 case is $9.43. Type the margin you need and the calculator prints the markup, 42.9% here, so nobody converts by hand.

faq.q: What does 5% markup mean?
faq.a: It means the price is the cost plus 5% of the cost. On a $22.00 case that adds $1.10, so the price is $23.10 and the margin is 4.8%. Five points of markup is always under five points of margin, and on food it will not cover shrink.

faq.q: What is a 40% markup on $100?
faq.a: The price is $140.00. The markup adds $40.00 to the $100.00 cost, and that $40.00 is a 28.6% margin on the $140.00 price. Type a $100.00 cost into the calculator and the 40% rung reads exactly that.

faq.q: What margin does a 20% markup leave?
faq.a: 16.7%, and it does not matter what the case cost. A $22.00 case at a 20% markup prices at $26.40 and keeps $4.40, which is 16.7% of $26.40. Type a $500.00 cost and the same rung prices at $600.00 and keeps $100.00, still 16.7%.

faq.q: Is 30% a good markup?
faq.a: On a $22.00 case a 30% markup prices at $28.60 and keeps 23.1%, which is thin once shrink and delivery come out of it. Name the margin you need first, then read the markup off the ladder. A 30% margin on that case takes 42.9%.

faq.q: How do you work out a selling price from a markup?
faq.a: Multiply the cost by one plus the markup. A $22.00 case at a 40% markup is $30.80, and at a 50% markup it is $33.00. Going the other way, divide the cost by one minus the margin, so $22.00 divided by 0.70 gives $31.43.

faq.q: How do you calculate retail margin?
faq.a: Subtract the cost from the shelf price, then divide by the shelf price. A $3.97 unit costing $2.38 keeps $1.59, and $1.59 divided by $3.97 is 40.1%. It reads 40.1% rather than 40.0% because an exact 40% needs $3.9667, and a real shelf tag settles that to $3.97.

faq.q: Is 50% margin the same as 100% markup?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the one place the two numbers meet. A 50% margin means half the shelf price is profit, so the profit equals the cost. On a $2.38 unit the price has to be $4.76, which keeps $2.38, and $2.38 on a $2.38 cost is a 100% markup. Above 50% margin the markup climbs much faster.

faq.q: What markup do I need for a 60% margin?
faq.a: A 150% markup. Divide 1 by 1 minus the margin and subtract 1, which turns 60% into 150%. On a $2.38 unit that is a $5.95 shelf price keeping $3.57, and $3.57 divided by $5.95 comes back to 60%. Set the target in the calculator and it prints the price for you.

faq.q: What is a good retail markup percentage?
faq.a: Most grocery categories run a 25% to 45% retail margin, which is a 33.3% to 81.8% markup on cost. Dry grocery sits at the bottom of that band and fresh or specialty sits at the top, because shrink eats into it. Quote the band for the category, then the dollars a case behind it.

faq.q: Is a 50% profit margin too much?
faq.a: It is high for grocery and normal in other categories. A 50% margin doubles the cost, so a $2.38 unit shelves at $4.76 instead of $3.97. Shoppers price-check against the next store, so that level usually holds only on specialty, prepared or slow-moving lines where nobody carries a reference price.

faq.q: What is contribution margin, and how is it calculated?
faq.a: Contribution margin is the price less the variable cost of selling one more unit. On this item the only variable cost is the $2.38, so contribution and gross profit are the same $1.59 a unit, or $19.08 a case. They separate once delivery, shrink or a promotion is counted, and none of those sit inside the 40.1%.

faq.q: What is a good profit margin for a food distributor?
faq.a: Gross and net are different questions, and this calculator answers neither for you. The 40.1% here is the store's gross margin on one unit. Judge an item on the dollars it earns, $19.08 a case and $9,540 a month at 500 cases, because a wide percentage on a slow unit is worth less than a thin one on a mover.

faq.q: How to calculate markup on food?
faq.a: Put the cost on the pounds you can sell, then mark that up. A $48.00 case at 40 lb and an 85% yield gives 34 usable lb, so cost is $1.41 a lb, and a 32% target margin prices it at $2.08. Mark up the $1.20 you paid per bought pound instead and you get $1.76, which leaves the trim unpaid for.

faq.q: How much mark up should you charge on food?
faq.a: Enough to cover the trim, not a round number off a chart. On this case $22.72 of gross profit against a $48.00 cost is a 47.3% markup, and the same $22.72 against $70.72 of revenue is a 32.1% margin. Decide the margin the line has to carry, then read off the markup it needs.

faq.q: Does trim belong in the cost or in the markup?
faq.a: In the cost, not the markup. Spread the $48.00 case over the 34 lb you can sell and cost is $1.41 a usable lb. Mark that up to $2.08. Price off the 40 lb you bought and the same target gives $1.76, which is $0.32 a lb short.

faq.q: How do you calculate food cost on product you cut yourself?
faq.a: Divide the case cost by the usable pounds, not the pounds on the invoice. $48.00 over 34 usable lb is $1.41, against $1.20 over the 40 lb you bought. The food cost percentage then comes off what the case really earns, so $48.00 of $70.72 is 67.9%.

faq.q: Is trim the same as shrink?
faq.a: No, and they belong in different places. Shrink is product you lose to spoilage, damage or a short count, and it goes into your landed cost. Trim is weight you never intended to sell, 6 lb of every 40 lb case here, and it belongs in the price per pound. Budgeting for one does not cover the other.

faq.q: How does yield change the price you need?
faq.a: Every point of yield you lose is carried by the pounds that are left. At an 85% yield this case needs $2.08 a lb. At 75% it needs $2.35, and at 90% it needs $1.96, a $0.39 spread on the same $48.00 case. Yield moves the price more than the case cost usually does.

faq.q: What yield should you use on a cut item?
faq.a: Your own, measured. Weigh the case in, weigh the saleable product out, and do it across a few cases and a few cutters. Assume 85% and really get 75% and you sell 30 lb at a price built for 34, so the case earns $62.40 instead of $70.72 and the margin goes with it.

faq.q: What is a standard wholesale markup?
faq.a: There is no single standard, and anyone quoting one is averaging across categories that behave nothing alike. Work it from your own landed cost instead. A 30% markup on a $22.00 case gives $28.60 and keeps $6.60, which is a 23.1% margin. Judge the margin, because the markup always sounds bigger than what you keep.

faq.q: What is keystone pricing?
faq.a: Keystone means the retailer doubles their cost. On a $2.38 unit that puts the shelf at $4.76 and leaves them a 50% margin. Grocery rarely keystones. At a 40% target the same unit shelves at $3.97, which is why the pack size and the target margin matter more than any rule of thumb.

faq.q: How do you work out the retail price from a wholesale price?
faq.a: Divide the case price by the units, then divide that by one minus the retail margin. A $28.60 case over 12 units is $2.38, and $2.38 divided by 0.60 is $3.97. Do not multiply by 1.40 instead, because that gives $3.33 and a 28.5% margin, not 40%.

faq.q: Why is the retailer's markup so much bigger than mine?
faq.a: You are each measuring against a different number. Your 30% is measured on your cost. Their 66.8% is what it takes, on top of your price, to leave 40% of the shelf price. Markup is always measured on cost, margin on the selling price.

faq.q: What margin does a grocery retailer need?
faq.a: It varies by category and by store format, so ask rather than assume. 40% is a common target on center store, and the calculator takes any figure you put in. Change it to 35% and the same case shelves at $3.67 instead of $3.97.

faq.q: Should I quote a case price or a unit price?
faq.a: Quote the case, but know the unit. Your buyer decides on the shelf price, and the shelf price comes from your case divided by the pack. Walking in with $28.60 and no idea it means $3.97 leaves you arguing about the wrong number.

faq.q: What happens to the shelf price when my cost goes up?
faq.a: It moves by more than your cost does. Every dollar you add to a case adds about $1.67 across the retail case, because the retailer takes their margin as a share of the shelf. A small freight increase you absorb is cheaper than one the shelf has to carry.

faq.q: How much volume can you lose after a price increase?
faq.a: More than most people expect. On a $30.00 case costing $22.00, a 5% increase lets you lose 15.8% of the volume and still match today's profit. That is the number to weigh an account's reaction against, rather than deciding on instinct.

faq.q: How do you work out the breakeven volume for a price change?
faq.a: Compare your contribution before and after. $30.00 less $22.00 is $8.00 today, and $31.50 less $22.00 is $9.50 after. Divide the old by the new and you keep 84.2% of the volume to break even, so you can lose 15.8%.

faq.q: Why does a small price increase move profit so much?
faq.a: Because the increase lands entirely on what you keep. 5% of a $30.00 price is $1.50, and that $1.50 goes straight onto $8.00 of contribution. The price moved 5% and your profit per case moved 18.8%.

faq.q: Is a price cut ever worth it?
faq.a: Sometimes, but it asks much more of volume than a raise gives back. A 5% cut takes contribution to $6.50 and needs 23.1% more cases just to hold profit. If the cut takes the price below your cost, no amount of volume can pay it back.

faq.q: Does the breakeven depend on how much you sell today?
faq.a: No, and that is what makes it useful. The breakeven is only the ratio of your old contribution to your new one, so 15.8% is the answer whether you move 600 cases a month or 60,000. Volume only changes the dollars, not the decision.

faq.q: Should you raise prices across the board or item by item?
faq.a: Item by item, because the same percentage does very different things to a thin line and a wide one. Run the thin lines first, since those are where a few cents of contribution change the breakeven most.

faq.q: How do you explain a price increase to an account?
faq.a: With the reason, the date and the number, in writing, before the invoice shows it. Say whether the move follows a cost increase or not. An account that hears it from a rep first argues less than one that finds it on a statement.

faq.q: What is PPV and how is it calculated?
faq.a: PPV is purchase price variance, the gap between the price you budgeted for an item and the price you were charged for it. Subtract the standard price from the actual price, then multiply by the cases you bought. $22.40 against a $22.00 standard across 6,000 cases is $2,400 unfavorable for the month.

faq.q: How do you calculate the purchase price variance (PPV)?
faq.a: Per item, per month, straight off the invoices. Pull every receipt line for that item, take the price each one charged, and set it against the $22.00 standard. Multiply the gap by the cases you received, not the cases you ordered. Hold the quantity still on both sides, because this answers price and nothing else.

faq.q: What is a good PPV value?
faq.a: There is no published benchmark, so judge it in dollars and by direction. A 1.8% gap reads like rounding and is $28,800 a year, which is worth a phone call. A good PPV is small, explained and shrinking, and a favorable one still needs a reason.

faq.q: What is the formula for price variance?
faq.a: Price variance is actual price less standard price, times the quantity you bought, which accounting also calls the material price variance. $0.40 times 6,000 cases is $2,400. This is the cost accounting kind of variance, not the statistical kind, so nothing here gets averaged or squared.

faq.q: What is the formula for PPV?
faq.a: PPV equals actual unit price less standard unit price, times units purchased. A positive answer is unfavorable, because you paid more than you planned. Pay $21.60 against the same $22.00 standard and the figure is $2,400 favorable, with actual spend at $129,600 rather than $134,400.

faq.q: What is a PPV calculation?
faq.a: It is a monthly check that your invoices match the prices you planned, run item by item. Here it holds $132,000 of spend at standard against the $134,400 you really spent. It is not a full cost variance calculation, because the quantity and the mix you bought are held still.

faq.q: How is MUV calculated?
faq.a: Material usage variance takes the quantity side: actual quantity less standard quantity, times the standard price. Price variance and usage variance split the same total gap between them, so run both before you blame the supplier. This tool does the price half, with the 6,000 cases held constant.

faq.q: What is an early payment discount?
faq.a: Points your supplier takes off the invoice if you pay before it is due. 2/10 net 30 means you keep 2% by paying inside 10 days on an invoice due in 30. On a $22.56 case that is $0.45, or $2,700 a month across 6,000 cases.

faq.q: What is the typical discount for early payment?
faq.a: Two percent inside ten days is the common one, and one percent inside ten days turns up almost as often. The points matter more than the window: 2% over 20 days annualizes to 37.2%, while 1% over the same 20 days is only 18.4%.

faq.q: What does 2% 10 net 30 mean?
faq.a: Keep 2% if you pay inside 10 days, or pay the full amount by day 30. All the discount buys is 20 days of float, which is why it is worth pricing as a rate. On this invoice that rate is 37.2% a year.

faq.q: How does a prompt pay discount work?
faq.a: The order of operations decides the number. Your volume discount comes off first, so $24.00 becomes $22.56, then the early pay discount comes off that for $22.11. Freight is added back last at $1.40 and never gets discounted.

faq.q: What are the four types of discounts?
faq.a: Trade or volume, cash or early pay, seasonal, and promotional. This calculator handles the first two, the 6% volume discount and the 2% early pay discount. Rebates paid back to you later belong on their own line, not inside the case price.

faq.q: How do you record an early payment discount in accounting?
faq.a: Your accountant decides where it lands, usually as a reduction of the purchase price rather than as income. The decision is the useful part. Taking 2/10 net 30 earns 37.2% a year on the cash, which beats what any credit line charges you.

faq.q: Are prompt pay discounts legal?
faq.a: Yes. An early payment discount is an ordinary commercial term you and your supplier agree, printed on the invoice as something like 2/10 net 30. Get it in writing alongside the volume tier, then check the remittance actually applied the 2% you took.

mainEntity.name: What is the typical discount for early payment?

mainEntity.name: What does 2% 10 net 30 mean?

mainEntity.name: How does a prompt pay discount work?

mainEntity.name: What are the four types of discounts?

mainEntity.name: How do you record an early payment discount in accounting?

faq.q: What is marginal cost?
faq.a: Marginal cost is the cost of moving one more case: the product, freight and handling, plus any new fixed cost the extra volume triggers, like an added route.

faq.q: How do you calculate marginal cost?
faq.a: Divide the change in total cost by the change in cases. Work out total cost before and after the new volume, including any step cost, subtract one from the other, then divide by the extra cases.

faq.q: What is the difference between marginal cost and average cost?
faq.a: Average cost spreads every cost across every case. Marginal cost counts only the next case, which is usually cheaper because your fixed costs are already covered by today's volume.

faq.q: Why does marginal cost matter for pricing?
faq.a: It sets the floor for new volume. As long as the price clears the marginal cost and covers any new route, the account makes you money, even when the price sits below your average cost.

faq.q: What is a step cost?
faq.a: A fixed cost that appears all at once when volume crosses a line, like a second truck, a driver or extra cooler space. It belongs in the marginal cost of the volume that triggered it.

faq.q: How can a distributor lower marginal cost?
faq.a: Fill the trucks and routes you already run before adding new ones, since an added truck raises the cost of every case on it until the volume catches up.

faq.q: Should you ever price below your average cost?
faq.a: Yes, when the price still clears the marginal cost and any step cost the volume adds. Below that floor the volume costs you money.

faq.q: What is a reorder point?
faq.a: The stock level that has to trigger your next order. It is the demand you will sell while you wait for the truck plus the buffer you keep, so 480 cases plus a 229 case buffer means you order at 709 cases on hand. It answers when to order, not how much to bring in.

faq.q: How is ROP calculated?
faq.a: Average daily usage times the lead time, plus the safety stock you already hold. 120 cases a day across 4 days is 480 cases, and a 229 case buffer takes the trigger to 709 cases. Measure the lead time from order placed to truck unloaded, because every extra day adds 120 cases.

faq.q: What is the formula for calculating reorder level?
faq.a: Reorder level, order point and ROP are three names for the same figure, usage across the lead time plus the buffer. Do not confuse it with a par level, which is the quantity you top up to. The reorder level is 709 cases here and says nothing about how much to order.

faq.q: What happens if the reorder point is too low?
faq.a: You run out before the truck arrives, and the buffer absorbs the gap until it cannot. A 2 day slip adds 240 cases of demand against a 229 case buffer, which leaves you 11 cases short. The answer is a trigger of 949 cases, not a call to the account on the day.

faq.q: How do you find the normal reorder period?
faq.a: Divide the trigger by your daily usage to see what it covers, then count down from today's stock. 709 cases is 5.9 days of cover at 120 cases a day, and 850 cases on hand leaves 1.2 days before you hit it. How often you order after that is set by how much you buy each time.

faq.q: What is the formula for calculating inventory level?
faq.a: Count what is on the floor, then hold it against the trigger. 850 cases on hand against a 709 case trigger leaves 141 cases of headroom, which is 1.2 days at 120 cases a day. If the count is a week old, so is the answer.

faq.q: How do you calculate the order point?
faq.a: Set it per line, then make sure somebody sees the count cross it. A trigger of 709 cases is worth nothing if stock gets checked once a week. Reset it whenever the lead time moves, since a 6 day lead time takes the same line to 949 cases.

faq.q: How do you calculate safety stock?
faq.a: Take the square root of the lead time times the demand swing squared, plus the demand squared times the lead time swing squared. That gives a combined swing of 138.92 cases here. Multiply it by the factor for your service level, 1.65 at 95%, and you get 229 cases.

faq.q: Is safety stock the same as a reorder point?
faq.a: No. Safety stock is the buffer itself, 229 cases here, sized from how much your demand and lead time vary. The reorder point is the level that triggers the order, 709 cases here, because it also counts the demand you will sell while you wait. This tool sizes the buffer, and a reorder point calculator tells you when to order.

faq.q: What is the 50% rule for safety stock?
faq.a: It sets the buffer at half the demand during lead time, which is 240 cases here against a real answer of 229. The agreement is luck. The rule never looks at how much your demand or your lead time varies, so when a supplier becomes reliable it still tells you to hold 240 cases.

faq.q: What service level should a food distributor use?
faq.a: 95% is a sensible starting point, and the last points get expensive quickly. Going from 95% to 99% adds 95 cases and $2,090. Going from 99% to 99.9% adds another 106 cases and $2,332, which is more money for about a fifth of the gain.

faq.q: Why does shelf life limit safety stock?
faq.a: Because buffer you cannot sell in time is spoilage. 229 cases is 1.9 days of cover against a 14 day shelf life, so it clears comfortably. Raise the service level far enough on a short life item and the buffer starts outliving the product.

faq.q: Does a bigger buffer always mean better service?
faq.a: No, and past a point it mostly means parked cash. A flat week of stock here is 840 cases and $18,480, which is $13,442 more than the 95% answer without fixing why you ran short. Fewer stockout surprises come from steadier lead times, not from a larger pile.

faq.q: What makes safety stock go up?
faq.a: Four things, and only one of them is demand. A wider demand swing, a longer lead time, a less reliable supplier and a higher service level all raise it. Supplier reliability is usually the cheapest of the four to fix.

acceptedAnswer.text: It sets the buffer at half the demand during lead time, which is 240 cases here against a real answer of 229. The agreement is luck. The rule never looks at how much your demand or your lead time varies, so when a supplier becomes reliable it still tells you to hold 240 cases.

mainEntity.name: What service level should a food distributor use?

acceptedAnswer.text: 95% is a sensible starting point, and the last points get expensive quickly. Going from 95% to 99% adds 95 cases and $2,090. Going from 99% to 99.9% adds another 106 cases and $2,332, which is more money for about a fifth of the gain.

mainEntity.name: Why does shelf life limit safety stock?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because buffer you cannot sell in time is spoilage. 229 cases is 1.9 days of cover against a 14 day shelf life, so it clears comfortably. Raise the service level far enough on a short life item and the buffer starts outliving the product.

mainEntity.name: Does a bigger buffer always mean better service?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, and past a point it mostly means parked cash. A flat week of stock here is 840 cases and $18,480, which is $13,442 more than the 95% answer without fixing why you ran short. Fewer stockout surprises come from steadier lead times, not from a larger pile.

mainEntity.name: What makes safety stock go up?

faq.q: What is a par level?
faq.a: The stock level you top a line back up to on every order cycle. It is the usage you will sell across the days you have to cover plus the buffer you carry, so 120 cases a day across 7 days between deliveries plus a 2 day buffer is a par level of 1,080 cases. faq.q: What is the par level formula?
faq.a: Average daily usage times the days you have to cover, where those days are your delivery cycle plus your buffer. Here that is 120 x 9, so 1,080 cases. The par level calculation rounds up to whole cases, and today's order is par less whatever the count says is on the floor.

faq.q: How is a par level different from a reorder point?
faq.a: A par level answers how much, and a reorder point answers when. Par here is 1,080 cases, the level the next delivery brings this line back to. faq.q: How do I calculate inventory turnover ratio?
faq.a: Divide annual cost of goods sold by average inventory, both at cost. $1,584,000 of cost of goods against $132,000 of average inventory gives 12.0 turns a year.

faq.q: What is the turnover ratio formula?
faq.a: Turnover equals cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. For days, divide 365 by the turnover: 365 divided by 12.0 is 30.4 days on hand.

faq.q: Is 1.5 a good inventory turnover ratio?
faq.a: Not for food distribution. At 1.5 turns a case sits about 243 days, which is far past the shelf life of most of what you carry. That figure comes from slower industries like heavy equipment.

faq.q: How many times should inventory be turned over per year?
faq.a: It depends on what you carry. Dry goods and canned stock often run 10 to 15 turns, while fresh and short-dated items need far more. Compare against your own last year before any benchmark.

faq.q: What is days inventory outstanding?
faq.a: The number of days an average case sits before it sells, which is 365 divided by your turnover. It is the same measure as turns, in a unit you can match against shelf life.

faq.q: What does slow inventory actually cost?
faq.a: Capital, space, insurance, spoilage and obsolescence. The 25% in the field is only a placeholder. Build the rate from your own five lines, as the inventory carrying cost calculator does, and it comes to 27%. The same $132,000 then costs $35,640 a year, not $33,000.

faq.q: How is this different from accounts receivable turnover?
faq.a: Inventory turnover measures how fast stock leaves the warehouse. Accounts receivable turnover measures how fast customers pay you for it. Both park cash, in different places.

faq.q: What are examples of carrying costs?
faq.a: Five lines you already pay: the cost of capital tied up in the stock, storage and handling, shrink and spoilage, insurance and taxes, and obsolescence. On $132,000 of average inventory they run $11,880, $9,240, $7,920, $2,640 and $3,960, which is $35,640 a year. The purchase cost of the goods is not one of them.

faq.q: What are the four types of inventory costs?
faq.a: Purchase cost, ordering cost, carrying cost and shortage cost. This tool does the third one only, so the $35,640 is what holding the stock costs you and not what buying it cost. Carrying cost is the one that never arrives as an invoice, which is why it gets left at a guess.

faq.q: What is the formula for calculating annual inventory carrying cost?
faq.a: Add the five component rates to get your carrying rate, then multiply it by average inventory at cost. 9 plus 7 plus 6 plus 2 plus 3 is 27%, and 27% of $132,000 is $35,640 a year. Use an average of twelve month end balances, because a peak month reads high.

faq.q: How to determine inventory carrying cost?
faq.a: Build it from the lines you already pay. Capital is what your credit line costs. Storage is rent plus racking plus the labor to touch a case twice, spoilage is last year's dump log over average inventory, insurance comes off the policy, and obsolescence is what you marked down to clear. Added up they are 9, 7, 6, 2 and 3 points, a 27% rate, which is $35,640 on $132,000 of average stock.

faq.q: What is the formula for calculating inventory cost?
faq.a: The inventory carrying cost formula is your carrying rate times average inventory value. Divide the answer by twelve for a month, $2,970 here, or by cases a year to cost one case. Inventory cost in the wider sense also carries the purchase price of the goods, which this leaves out on purpose.

faq.q: How much inventory should you carry?
faq.a: Less than feels comfortable, because every dollar of average stock costs you 27 cents a year. Taking average inventory down 10% to $118,800 saves $3,564 a year and no price has to change. Set the floor on the service you owe your accounts, then stop.

faq.q: What is the 80/20 rule in inventory?
faq.a: Roughly a fifth of your items carry most of the inventory value, so price those first. The rate is the same across the warehouse, but it lands unevenly: the lines that sit longest pay the spoilage and obsolescence points hardest, 6 points and 3 points of the 27. Work the top of that list and the $35,640 moves.

faq.q: How do you calculate the warehouse space you need?
faq.a: Turn cases into pallets, pallets into floor positions, then add the aisles. 3,000 cases at 50 a pallet is 60 pallets. Stacked two high that is 30 positions, and 30 positions at 13.3 sq ft is 399 sq ft of product. Add 45% for aisles, dock and staging and you need 725 sq ft.

faq.q: How much space do 3,000 cases need?
faq.a: About 725 sq ft stacked two high, which works out at 0.24 sq ft a case. That figure moves a long way with stack height. The same 3,000 cases fit in 484 sq ft at three high.

faq.q: Should you size for peak inventory or average?
faq.a: Peak. The average never has to fit through the door at once. Size on the high-water mark, because the few weeks you are over it are exactly when overflow storage is hardest to find and costs the most.

faq.q: How many cases fit on a pallet?
faq.a: 50 is a fair default for dry goods, and it moves with case size and stacking strength. It matters more than it looks. Ten more cases a pallet takes 60 pallets down to 50, which is five fewer floor positions and 120 sq ft less building.

faq.q: Does stacking higher cut the space you need?
faq.a: More than anything else you can change. Two high to three takes 725 sq ft down to 484, a 33.2% saving, because you are using height you already pay rent on. Check your racking rating and your ceiling before you count on it.

faq.q: How much should you add for growth?
faq.a: Work it in cases, not as a percentage of floor. Let peak drift from 3,000 cases to 3,600 and the space goes from 725 sq ft to 871. Put the peak you expect straight into the calculator rather than padding the answer at the end.

faq.q: Does turning stock faster cut the space you need?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the cheapest way to do it. The space is driven by cases on hand at peak, so anything that lowers the peak lowers the building. Ordering smaller and more often cuts the number without touching a wall.

acceptedAnswer.text: About 725 sq ft stacked two high, which works out at 0.24 sq ft a case. That figure moves a long way with stack height. The same 3,000 cases fit in 484 sq ft at three high.

mainEntity.name: Should you size for peak inventory or average?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peak. The average never has to fit through the door at once. Size on the high-water mark, because the few weeks you are over it are exactly when overflow storage is hardest to find and costs the most.

mainEntity.name: How many cases fit on a pallet?

acceptedAnswer.text: 50 is a fair default for dry goods, and it moves with case size and stacking strength. It matters more than it looks. Ten more cases a pallet takes 60 pallets down to 50, which is five fewer floor positions and 120 sq ft less building.

mainEntity.name: Does stacking higher cut the space you need?

acceptedAnswer.text: More than anything else you can change. Two high to three takes 725 sq ft down to 484, a 33.2% saving, because you are using height you already pay rent on. Check your racking rating and your ceiling before you count on it.

mainEntity.name: How much should you add for growth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Work it in cases, not as a percentage of floor. Let peak drift from 3,000 cases to 3,600 and the space goes from 725 sq ft to 871. Put the peak you expect straight into the calculator rather than padding the answer at the end.

mainEntity.name: Does turning stock faster cut the space you need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and it is the cheapest way to do it. The space is driven by cases on hand at peak, so anything that lowers the peak lowers the building. Ordering smaller and more often cuts the number without touching a wall.

faq.q: How do you calculate the cost per delivery?
faq.a: Add the driver, the fuel and the truck for one day, then divide by the stops. A $28.00 driver over 8 hours is $224.00, 120 miles at 8 mpg is $61.50 of fuel at $4.10, and the truck day is $95.00. That $380.50 across 14 drops is $27.18 a delivery.

faq.q: Where should a delivery minimum be set?
faq.a: Above the margin a stop has to earn, not at a round number. At $27.18 a drop, an account buying at a 20% margin has to order $135.90 of product before the stop pays for itself. Set the minimum so the smallest order on the truck still clears that.

faq.q: Should you charge customers for delivery?
faq.a: Either charge for it or price it in, but do it knowing the number. At $0.54 a case, a 50 case drop absorbs the stop without anyone noticing. At $2.72 a case, a 10 case drop does not, so that is where a delivery charge or a minimum belongs.

faq.q: What does a light drop do to your margin?
faq.a: It takes it a case at a time. The same $27.18 stop spread over 10 cases is $2.72 a case against a $0.91 route average. If the gross margin on those cases is under $2.72, the delivery costs more than the order earns.

faq.q: Should you drop an account that orders too little?
faq.a: Change the frequency or the minimum before you drop it. An account taking a stop every week at 10 cases can take one every other week at 20 cases, and the route cost falls from $2.72 a case to $1.36 with the same volume sold.

faq.q: How do you count the truck's fixed cost in a delivery cost?
faq.a: As a cost per route day, not a cost per mile. Take the lease or depreciation, insurance, maintenance and plates for the year, then divide by the days the truck actually runs. At $95.00 a day that is 25.0% of a $380.50 route before the truck leaves the yard.

faq.q: What is the cost per case on a delivery route?
faq.a: Route cost over the cases that route carries. $380.50 across 420 cases is $0.91 a case, and $3.17 a mile across 120 miles. Load 840 cases on the same day and the case cost falls to $0.45, while the cost per drop stays at $27.18.

pain_cards.body: It is in the price somewhere. At $27.18 a drop, the big orders are quietly paying for the small ones, and nobody has priced that choice.

tools_cards.title: Fuel and mpg

tools_cards.body: The same $380.50 over 14 stops is $27.18 each. Fewer stops in the day means a dearer stop, with nothing else changing.

tools_cards.title: Cases per drop

tools_cards.title: Order accuracy
tools_cards.body: A wrong case is a second trip, and a second trip costs the full $27.18 again. Order accuracy is a route cost, not an office cost.

faq.q: What is the formula for accounts receivable turnover?
faq.a: Annual credit sales divided by average accounts receivable. $9,600,000 of credit sales against an average book of $1,020,000 gives 9.4 turns a year.

faq.q: What is the turnover of accounts receivable?
faq.a: It is how many times a year you collect your whole receivables book. Nine point four turns means the average invoice is paid and replaced about every 39 days.

faq.q: What is a good AR turnover ratio?
faq.a: Judge it against your own terms rather than a benchmark. On net 30 a ratio near 12 means you collect on time; 9.4 means you are running 8.8 days behind what you wrote.

faq.q: What is days sales outstanding?
faq.a: The average days from invoice to cash, which is 365 divided by your turnover. It is the same measure as the ratio, in the unit your terms are written in.

faq.q: Why use credit sales instead of total sales?
faq.a: Cash and card sales never become receivables. Counting them inflates the numerator and makes a slow book look faster than it is.

faq.q: What does slow collection actually cost?
faq.a: The cash sits elsewhere and you finance the gap. At 8.8 days past terms that is $230,959 of your money, costing $20,786 a year at a 9% cost of money.

faq.q: How is this different from inventory turnover?
faq.a: Receivables turnover measures how fast customers pay you. Inventory turnover measures how fast stock leaves the warehouse. Both park cash, in different places.
